templates.name: Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Present or describe to an already familiar audience
Specify or identify a single fact

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the third century CE, Chinese engineers constructed the south-pointing chariot, a two-wheeled vehicle topped by a carved figure.
• Unlike a compass, the chariot used no magnets; before departure, its operator set the figure’s arm to point south.
• An arrangement of interlocking gears connected the figure to both wheels.
• During a turn, the chariot’s outer wheel traveled farther than its inner wheel.
• The gears translated this difference into an equal rotation of the figure in the opposite direction, keeping its arm pointed southward.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how the south-pointing chariot kept its figure pointing south. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Built by Chinese engineers in the third century CE, the south-pointing chariot used no magnets, relying instead on an operator who set its figure to point south before departure.
Gears connecting the figure to both wheels kept the wheels traveling equal distances during every turn, so the figure never rotated and its arm continued to point south.
During a turn, gears linked to both wheels rotated the figure in the opposite direction by an amount matching how much farther the outer wheel traveled, keeping the arm pointed south.
Whenever the chariot turned, its outer wheel traveled farther than its inner wheel, and the operator then used the gears to turn the figure back toward the south.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain how the chariot kept its figure pointing south. The notes give a chain: gears “connected the figure to both wheels,” “During a turn, the chariot’s outer wheel traveled farther than its inner wheel,” and “The gears translated this difference into an equal rotation of the figure in the opposite direction.” Choice C follows that whole chain from the turn to the figure’s matching counterturn.

A.recipe: OG (what the device is and how it was set up, not how it kept pointing)
A.why_wrong: It describes the chariot and how the operator set the figure “before departure,” but it never explains what kept the figure pointing south once the chariot began turning.

B.why_wrong: It explains a mechanism, but the notes say “the chariot’s outer wheel traveled farther than its inner wheel,” so the wheels did not travel equal distances, and the figure did rotate.

D.why_wrong: It credits the operator with turning the figure during the journey, but the notes say the operator only set the arm “before departure”; the gears did the turning.

items.notes: Subject: history of technology (the south-pointing chariot, a real non-magnetic Chinese device; mechanism stated as in modern gear reconstructions; no named people). Band 6 (EXPL has band-7 officials but the plan sets 6): how-goal over a three-bullet chain; two goal-shaped FALSE options (B denies the wheel difference, D swaps the agent) and one OG setup option.

fixes: notes trimmed toward CB length (traveled farther than); quotes in explanation and B updated

band7.why: Planned band 6 (EXPL has band-7 officials, the plan set 6). How-goal over a three-bullet chain with two goal-shaped FALSE options (B denies the wheel difference, D gives the turning to the operator) and one OG setup option; the key paraphrases the chain rather than copying it. A strong band 6.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Floating solar farms are photovoltaic panels mounted on platforms that float on reservoirs.
• In a 2021 study, engineers compared panels on a floating solar farm with identical panels installed on nearby land.
• The floating panels generated 6% more electricity than the land-based panels.
• Water beneath the floating panels lost 40% less to evaporation than open water nearby.
• The engineers attributed the higher output to the water, which kept the floating panels cooler.
items.stem: The student wants to present the findings of the study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The engineers found that the floating panels generated more electricity than identical panels on land and that the water beneath them lost less to evaporation.
According to the 2021 study, the floating panels generated 40% more electricity than identical land-based panels because the water kept them cooler.
The engineers found that the floating panels generated 6% more electricity and cut the reservoir’s total evaporation by 40%.
Engineers compared panels on a floating solar farm with identical panels installed on nearby land to learn whether the water beneath them would affect how much electricity they produced.
items.explanation: The study had two findings: the floating panels “generated 6% more electricity than the land-based panels,” and water beneath them “lost 40% less to evaporation than open water nearby.” Choice A presents both findings accurately, dropping the figures rather than misattaching them.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: number attached to the wrong finding)
B.why_wrong: It moves the 40% figure from evaporation to electricity; the notes say the floating panels “generated 6% more electricity,” and it leaves out the evaporation finding.

C.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: scope shift of a figure)
C.why_wrong: It presents both findings but misstates the second: only water “beneath the floating panels” lost 40% less to evaporation than open water nearby, not the whole reservoir.

D.why_wrong: It describes how the study was set up and what the engineers wanted to learn, but it reports no result: neither the higher output nor the reduced evaporation appears, so it does not present the findings.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (floating solar panels). Unnamed, generic study with invented figures (WAVE.md: invented numbers only on an unnamed, plainly generic study). Band 7 moves (from 5645f119, without its Finding labels or key frame): two numeric findings, key drops the numbers, two goal-shaped FALSE options misattach or rescope them, one PART that gives method plus interpretation.

band7.why: Follows 5645f119: two numeric findings, the key drops both numbers, B moves the 40% to electricity and C rescopes the evaporation figure to the whole reservoir (two goal-shaped FALSE options), and D gives method plus one finding, incomplete like the model’s A.

items.safety_fix: 2026-10-27 lead: safety judged old D defensible (it reported the higher output inside the engineers' explanation). D rebuilt as method plus aim with no result.

safety.unfair: D also presents a study finding (higher output) plus the engineers' attributed cause; it is not just the method, so the method-only distractor does not cleanly fail the goal.
safety.lead_override: 2026-10-27 lead: safety and gate run 2 found old D defensible; D rebuilt as method plus aim with no result (see safety_fix). Key A stands.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cowrie shells, produced by a small marine snail, circulated as currency throughout parts of Africa and Asia for centuries.
• Many of these shells were harvested in the shallow lagoons of the Maldives, an archipelago in the Indian Ocean.
• Beginning in the 1500s, European merchants purchased enormous quantities of the shells at ports in India.
• They transported the shells to West Africa, frequently using them as ballast to stabilize their ships.
• In West African markets, cowries purchased everyday goods and settled debts.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the cowrie shell trade. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In West African markets, cowrie shells, which arrived aboard European ships, were used to purchase everyday goods and to settle debts.
Beginning in the 1500s, European merchants harvested cowrie shells in West African lagoons and transported them as ballast to the Maldives, where the shells then circulated as currency.
Cowrie shells, which are produced by a small marine snail, circulated as currency for centuries throughout parts of both Africa and Asia.
Harvested in the Maldives and purchased by European merchants in India, cowrie shells were shipped to West Africa, where they served as money in markets.
items.explanation: An overview of the trade has to follow the shells from start to finish. The notes say the shells “were harvested in the shallow lagoons of the Maldives,” that European merchants “purchased enormous quantities of the shells at ports in India,” that “They transported the shells to West Africa,” and that there “cowries purchased everyday goods.” Choice D covers each stage in one sentence.

A.why_wrong: It covers only how the shells were used once they reached West Africa; it leaves out where they were gathered and bought.

B.why_wrong: It sketches the whole route, but backward: the shells were harvested in the Maldives and transported “to West Africa,” not harvested in West Africa and carried to the Maldives.

C.why_wrong: It says what cowrie shells are and where they served as money, but it says nothing about the trade that carried them from the Maldives to West Africa.

items.notes: Subject: history (the cowrie shell trade from the Maldives via Indian ports to West Africa; real, well-documented; no named people). Band 6 shape of the commodity-chain model 3.8 (PART one end, OG definition) plus one goal-shaped FALSE with the route reversed.

band7.why: Planned band 6. OVERVIEW band-6 shape (PART one end of the chain, OG background on cowries) plus a goal-shaped FALSE with the route reversed, as section 5 asks; every stage of the key needs three bullets combined.

items.subtype: Contrast on a non-obvious dimension (what shapes each)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Approaching the Sun, a comet releases gas and dust, which can form two distinct tails.
• The dust tail consists of microscopic solid particles pushed gently outward by the pressure of sunlight.
• Traveling slowly, these particles gradually lag behind the comet, so the dust tail curves along its trajectory.
• The ion tail consists of electrically charged gas accelerated by the solar wind, the Sun’s outflowing stream of particles.
• Consequently, this tail remains perfectly straight, pointing directly away from the Sun.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how the two tails get their shapes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: While sunlight sweeps a comet’s ion tail into a straight line pointing away from the Sun, the solar wind pushes the dust tail’s particles into a curve along the comet’s trajectory.
Whereas sunlight gently pushes the dust tail’s slow particles, which lag behind the comet in a curve, the solar wind drives the ion tail straight away from the Sun.
A comet’s two tails differ in their composition: the dust tail is made of microscopic solid particles, while the ion tail is made of electrically charged gas.
Whereas the dust tail curves because sunlight pushes its particles faster than the comet travels, the ion tail stays straight because the solar wind drives its charged gas directly away from the Sun.
items.explanation: To contrast how the tails get their shapes, a sentence must give each tail’s cause and result. The notes say the dust tail’s particles are “pushed gently outward by the pressure of sunlight” and “gradually lag behind the comet, so the dust tail curves,” while the ion tail is “accelerated by the solar wind” and “remains perfectly straight, pointing directly away from the Sun.” Choice B sets these side by side.

A.why_wrong: It makes the right kind of contrast but swaps the causes: the notes say sunlight pushes the dust tail and “the solar wind” accelerates the ion tail.

C.recipe: REL (true difference on the wrong dimension)
C.why_wrong: It contrasts what the tails are made of, which the notes do state, but it does not say how either tail gets its shape.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: right forces, reason for the dust tail’s curve reversed)
D.why_wrong: It names the right force for each tail, but it misstates why the dust tail curves: the notes say the particles are “Traveling slowly” and “gradually lag behind the comet,” not that sunlight pushes them faster than the comet travels.

items.notes: Subject: science (comet dust and ion tails, astronomy well known to me; no figures or people). Band 7 moves: the compared dimension is the cause of each shape, not composition or color; A is goal-shaped and false (agents swapped), C is a true difference on the wrong dimension (459df2ba C pattern), D (rewritten at review) is a second goal-shaped FALSE with the right forces but the dust tail’s reason reversed. Background knowledge agrees with the notes, so it cannot rescue a wrong option.

fixes: D was a vague both-plus option no student keeps; rewritten as a second goal-shaped FALSE (right forces, the dust tail’s curve credited to particles moving faster than the comet, against “Traveling slowly”), so two FALSE options die on different bullets

band7.why: After the fix. The compared dimension is the cause of each shape; A swaps the two forces and the new D keeps the forces but reverses why the dust tail curves (the notes say its particles are traveling slowly and lag), so two goal-shaped FALSE options die on different bullets, and C is a true difference on the wrong dimension (composition). Before the fix D was a vague both-plus option no student keeps, which read band 6. Comet tails are classroom astronomy, but every fact needed is in the notes, so background knowledge only confirms them.

items.subtype: Use a quotation to emphasize a risk
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Assisted migration is the deliberate relocation of species to regions whose future climate is expected to suit them.
• Some foresters now transplant seedlings hundreds of miles north of their current ranges.
• Forest ecologist Ingrid Solberg argues that the practice could help trees “keep pace with a climate shifting faster than their seeds can travel.”
• Conservation biologist Rafael Quintero acknowledges that the practice “has won over many land managers.”
• But he warns that a relocated species “may thrive too well, crowding out the plants and animals already living there.”
items.stem: The student wants to use a quotation to emphasize a potential risk of assisted migration. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Solberg argues that trees need help to “keep pace with a climate shifting faster than their seeds can travel,” a problem that assisted migration could address.
Although Quintero warns that relocated species could crowd out the plants and animals already living in their new regions, he acknowledges that assisted migration “has won over many land managers.”
Quintero cautions that a species relocated through assisted migration “may thrive too well, crowding out the plants and animals already living there.”
Planting seedlings hundreds of miles north of their current ranges could harm the plants and animals already living in those regions if the newcomers spread too widely.
items.explanation: The goal calls for a quotation that points to a risk of assisted migration itself. Quintero warns that a relocated species “may thrive too well, crowding out the plants and animals already living there.” Choice C quotes exactly those words and ties them to assisted migration.

A.why_wrong: It quotes Solberg on a problem trees face from a fast-shifting climate, a problem the practice is meant to solve, not a risk of the practice.

B.recipe: NOQ (risk in the writer’s own words, quotation on popularity)
B.why_wrong: It mentions the risk only in its own words; the words it quotes, that the practice “has won over many land managers,” stress how popular assisted migration has become, and that popularity is the sentence’s main point.

D.why_wrong: It describes a risk the notes support, but it uses no quotation, which the goal requires.

items.notes: Subject: science and conservation (assisted migration, a real practice). Ingrid Solberg and Rafael Quintero are invented names with invented quotations (RS: no fact-checking); each was searched once and no ecologist or conservation biologist with the name turned up. No QUOTE item sits at band 7, so written as a strong band 6 (WAVE.md): A quotes a problem the practice addresses, B (rewritten at review, e8494245 B pattern) names the risk in its own words but quotes Quintero on popularity, D does the goal's job without a quotation.

fixes: notes trimmed toward CB length (now transplant, the practice, But he warns)
B quoted popularity alone and its why_wrong called Quintero “the critic”; B now paraphrases the risk and quotes the popularity line (e8494245 B pattern), why_wrong rewritten
invented names searched once (Ingrid Solberg, Rafael Quintero): no real person in the field turned up; no change

band7.why: No QUOTE item sits at band 7, so it cannot be band 7. Hardened to a strong band 6 on the e8494245 pattern: B now states the risk in its own words but quotes the popularity line, A quotes the benefit, D states the risk with no quotation.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mason bees and wool carder bees are solitary: each female builds and stocks her own nest.
• Both often nest inside hollow plant stems or old beetle tunnels.
• A mason bee divides her nest into chambers with walls of mud.
• A wool carder bee lines each chamber with soft hairs she scrapes from leaves.
• In each chamber, the female leaves a ball of pollen and lays a single egg.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the nests of mason bees and those of wool carder bees. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Whereas mason bees separate the chambers of their nests with walls of mud, wool carder bees line theirs with soft hairs scraped from leaves.
Mason bees and wool carder bees both nest inside hollow plant stems, and in each chamber the female leaves a ball of pollen and lays a single egg.
A female mason bee builds her own nest, dividing it into separate chambers with walls of mud.
As solitary insects, mason bees and wool carder bees each build nests, though they do not build them in the same way.
items.explanation: To emphasize a difference, the sentence must contrast the two nests on the same feature. The notes say a mason bee divides her nest into chambers “with walls of mud,” while a wool carder bee “lines each chamber with soft hairs she scrapes from leaves.” Choice A sets these two building materials against each other with “Whereas.”

B.why_wrong: It describes what the two nests have in common, the hollow stems and the pollen and egg in each chamber, so it emphasizes a similarity.

C.why_wrong: It describes only the mason bee’s nest, so there is nothing to contrast it with.

D.why_wrong: It says the bees construct their nests differently but never says how.

items.notes: Subject: science (mason bees, Osmia, and the wool carder bee, Anthidium manicatum, which lines its cells with plant hairs; common biology, no named people). Replaced at review: the leafcutter side repeated the live Central Ideas item on leafcutter bee nests built from cut leaves. Parallel-pair arc with one shared trait (stems, pollen and egg) for the REL option.

fixes: leafcutter bees replaced by wool carder bees: a live Central Ideas item (central_ideas_and_details.T1.easy) is about leafcutter bee nests built from cut leaves; new pair grepped and claimed
notes plained and trimmed (builds and stocks, divides her nest into chambers, old beetle tunnels, leaves a ball of pollen)

items.subtype: Emphasize how X differs from Y
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Painting conservators sometimes fill damaged areas with new paint, a process called inpainting.
• In invisible inpainting, new paint matches the original so precisely that the repair cannot be detected.
• Tratteggio, a technique developed in Rome in the mid-1900s, fills gaps with fine vertical lines of pure color.
• From a distance, these lines blend into the surrounding image.
• Up close, however, viewers can distinguish restored areas from original ones.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how tratteggio differs from invisible inpainting. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Inpainting, the process of filling gaps in damaged paintings with new paint, is something conservators can do in more than one way.
Like invisible inpainting, tratteggio produces repairs that blend into the surrounding image when seen from a distance.
Developed in Rome in the mid-1900s, tratteggio fills gaps in damaged paintings with fine vertical lines of pure color.
Unlike invisible inpainting, whose repairs cannot be detected, tratteggio leaves repairs that viewers can spot up close.
items.explanation: The difference the notes set up is visibility. In invisible inpainting “the repair cannot be detected,” whereas with tratteggio, “Up close, however, viewers can distinguish restored areas from original ones.” Choice D contrasts the two methods on exactly this point.

A.why_wrong: It defines inpainting in general and says it can be done in different ways, but it never says how tratteggio differs from invisible inpainting.

B.why_wrong: It points out something the two methods share, that from a distance the repair blends in, so it emphasizes a similarity.

C.why_wrong: It describes tratteggio alone and never compares it with invisible inpainting.

items.notes: Subject: arts (tratteggio, a real painting-conservation method developed in Rome in the mid-twentieth century; no named people). The distance bullet gives a true shared trait for the REL option.

fixes: notes trimmed toward the models’ median (fill damaged areas, a process called inpainting)

items.subtype: Describe a work to an audience unfamiliar with the artist
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Magdalena Abakanowicz (1930–2017) was an influential Polish sculptor.
• She first gained recognition in the 1960s for enormous hanging sculptures woven from natural fibers such as sisal.
• Her installation Agora (2006) occupies a section of Grant Park in Chicago, Illinois.
• It consists of 106 cast-iron figures, each approximately nine feet tall.
• The figures lack heads and arms, and their surfaces are deeply textured, resembling tree bark.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Agora to an audience unfamiliar with Magdalena Abakanowicz. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The 106 cast-iron figures of Agora, which occupies a section of Chicago’s Grant Park, lack heads and arms.
Agora, a 2006 work by Polish sculptor Magdalena Abakanowicz, consists of 106 headless, armless cast-iron figures in Chicago’s Grant Park.
Polish sculptor Magdalena Abakanowicz first gained recognition in the 1960s for enormous hanging sculptures woven from natural fibers.
Abakanowicz’s Agora, which stands in Chicago’s Grant Park, consists of 106 nine-foot cast-iron figures whose textured surfaces resemble tree bark.
items.explanation: An audience unfamiliar with Abakanowicz needs to be told who she is as well as what Agora looks like. Choice B identifies her as a “Polish sculptor” and describes the installation’s “106 cast-iron figures,” which “lack heads and arms.”

A.why_wrong: It describes Agora but never says who made it, so a new audience learns nothing about Abakanowicz.

C.why_wrong: It introduces Abakanowicz but describes her 1960s fiber sculptures, not Agora.

D.why_wrong: It describes Agora well but uses Abakanowicz’s name as if the audience already knew who she was.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Magdalena Abakanowicz and Agora, Grant Park, Chicago, 2006; facts I know well: 106 headless, armless cast-iron figures about nine feet tall; Abakans woven from sisal and other fibers). Two AUD options as in 2.36.

items.subtype: Introduce a concept to an unfamiliar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Universal design is an approach that aims to make buildings and products accessible to as many people as possible.
• American architect Ronald Mace introduced the term in the 1980s.
• One example is the curb cut, a small ramp connecting a sidewalk to the street.
• Originally intended for wheelchair users, curb cuts also benefit pedestrians pushing strollers.
• Lever door handles, which are easier to grip than round knobs, are another example.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce universal design to an audience unfamiliar with the concept. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Curb cuts, small ramps connecting sidewalks to streets, benefit wheelchair users as well as pedestrians pushing strollers.
American architect Ronald Mace introduced the term “universal design” in the 1980s.
Universal design, an approach that aims to make buildings and products accessible to as many people as possible, includes features like curb cuts.
Like lever door handles, which are easier to grip than round knobs, curb cuts, the small ramps connecting sidewalks to streets, are an example of universal design.
items.explanation: An audience unfamiliar with universal design needs to know what it is. Choice C explains that it is “an approach that aims to make buildings and products accessible to as many people as possible” and then gives a familiar example, the curb cut.

A.why_wrong: It describes curb cuts but never mentions universal design, so the audience is not introduced to the concept.

B.why_wrong: It says who introduced the term but not what universal design is.

D.why_wrong: It uses the term “universal design” as if the audience already understood it, offering examples without saying what the approach is.

items.notes: Subject: social science and design (universal design; the term coined by architect Ronald Mace in the 1980s, which I know well). Concept-introduction shape of 2.43: two AUD options and one OG.

fixes: notes trimmed toward the models’ median (two curb-cut bullets shortened)

items.subtype: Explain the origin of a name
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Vanadium is a hard, silvery metal often added to steel to strengthen it.
• In 1801, mineralogist Andrés Manuel del Río identified the element in Mexico, naming it erythronium because its salts turned red when heated.
• Other chemists persuaded him it was impure chromium.
• In 1830, Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefström rediscovered it.
• He named it for Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds come in many brilliant colors.
items.stem: The student wants to explain the origin of vanadium’s name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Del Río named the element erythronium because its salts turned red when heated, though other chemists believed it was only impure chromium.
Vanadium, a hard, silvery metal often added to steel, was rediscovered in 1830 by Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefström.
The name vanadium, which was chosen by Sefström in 1830, has a different origin from the name that del Río had given the element.
Sefström named vanadium for Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, because the element’s compounds come in many brilliant colors.
items.explanation: To explain the origin of the name, a sentence must say what it honors and why. The notes say Sefström “named it for Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds come in many brilliant colors.” Choice D gives both the source of the name and the reason for it.

A.why_wrong: It explains where the name erythronium came from, del Río’s earlier name for the element, not the name vanadium.

B.why_wrong: It says what vanadium is and who rediscovered it, but not where its name came from.

C.why_wrong: It says the name has its own origin but never says what that origin is.

items.notes: Subject: science and history (the naming of vanadium; del Río’s erythronium of 1801 and Sefström’s 1830 name after Vanadís, both well known to me). Trap: A explains the origin of the element’s other name.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the 1700s, shipworms, wood-boring clams, severely damaged the hulls of many wooden vessels.
• Seaweed and barnacles also accumulated on hulls, slowing ships considerably.
• In the 1760s, Britain’s Royal Navy began fastening thin copper sheets to the underwater portions of its ships.
• Copper is toxic to shipworms and to many of the organisms that attach themselves to hulls.
• By the 1780s, the majority of Royal Navy ships had copper-sheathed hulls.
items.stem: The student wants to explain an advantage of covering ships’ hulls with copper. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Because copper is toxic to shipworms and to many organisms that attach themselves to hulls, copper sheets protected ships from damage and from growths that slowed them.
In the 1760s, Britain’s Royal Navy began fastening thin copper sheets to the underwater portions of its wooden ships.
Shipworms, wood-boring clams, severely damaged ships’ wooden hulls, while seaweed and barnacles accumulated on the hulls and slowed the ships.
By the 1780s, the majority of the ships in Britain’s Royal Navy had copper-sheathed hulls, a change that the navy had first begun to make in the 1760s.
items.explanation: An advantage has to link the copper to a benefit. The notes say “Copper is toxic to shipworms and to many of the organisms that attach themselves to hulls,” and that shipworms “severely damaged the hulls” while seaweed and barnacles were “slowing ships considerably.” Choice A connects the copper to protection from both problems.

B.why_wrong: It says when and how the navy started using copper sheets but not what the copper did for the ships.

C.why_wrong: It describes the damage and slowing that ships suffered but never mentions copper, so it gives no advantage of it.

D.why_wrong: It says how far the practice spread in the navy, not why copper helped.

items.notes: Subject: history of technology (copper sheathing of Royal Navy hulls from the 1760s; widespread by the 1780s; well known to me). Problem-without-solution PART option as in 2.3 C.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm are best known for their collections of fairy tales.
• In 1838, they began compiling the Deutsches Wörterbuch, a dictionary documenting the history of every German word.
• Wilhelm died in 1859, having completed the entries for the letter D.
• Jacob died in 1863, partway through the entry for Frucht (fruit).
• Successive generations of scholars continued the project, finally completing it in 1961.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how long it took to complete the dictionary. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Jacob Grimm died in 1863 while writing the Deutsches Wörterbuch’s entry for Frucht, four years after the death of his brother Wilhelm.
Begun by the Grimm brothers in 1838, the Deutsches Wörterbuch was not completed until 1961, more than a century later.
Best known for their fairy tales, Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm also began compiling a dictionary documenting the history of every German word.
After the deaths of both Grimm brothers, successive generations of scholars continued their work on a dictionary of the German language.
items.explanation: To emphasize how long the dictionary took, a sentence should give its start and finish. The notes say the brothers began it “In 1838” and that later scholars finished it “in 1961.” Choice B gives both dates and stresses the span with “not completed until” and “more than a century later.”

A.why_wrong: It gives the dates of the brothers’ deaths, which do not show how long the whole project took.

C.recipe: OG (who began it and what it covers)
C.why_wrong: It says what the dictionary traces and who began it, but nothing about how long it took to finish.

D.why_wrong: It hints that the work went on for a long time but gives neither when it began nor when it was finished.

items.notes: Subject: humanities and history (the Grimms' Deutsches Wörterbuch, begun 1838, finished 1961; Wilhelm wrote D, Jacob died at Frucht; well known to me). An official Boundaries item mentions the Grimms' fairy tales, a different subject.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Completed in 2013, the Great Tapestry of Scotland is an embroidered artwork depicting the history of Scotland.
• Novelist Alexander McCall Smith conceived the project, and artist Andrew Crummy designed it.
• It consists of 160 panels stitched by approximately 1,000 volunteers.
• Placed end to end, the panels extend 143 meters (469 feet).
• Since 2021, it has been permanently exhibited in Galashiels, a town in the Scottish Borders.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the length of the Great Tapestry of Scotland. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Approximately 1,000 volunteers stitched the panels of the Great Tapestry of Scotland, an embroidered artwork depicting the history of Scotland.
Conceived by novelist Alexander McCall Smith, the Great Tapestry of Scotland was designed by artist Andrew Crummy.
Placed end to end, the 160 panels of the Great Tapestry of Scotland extend a remarkable 143 meters (469 feet).
Since 2021, the Great Tapestry of Scotland has been permanently exhibited in Galashiels, a town in the Scottish Borders.
items.explanation: The goal is to emphasize length. The notes say that “Placed end to end, the panels extend 143 meters (469 feet).” Choice C gives that measurement and stresses it with “a remarkable.”

A.recipe: OG (who made it and what it shows)
A.why_wrong: It says how many volunteers stitched the work and what it depicts, not how long it is.

B.why_wrong: It names the people who conceived and designed the work but says nothing about its length.

D.why_wrong: It tells where the work is displayed, not how long it is.

items.notes: Subject: arts (the Great Tapestry of Scotland, 160 panels, about 143 m, about 1,000 stitchers, displayed in Galashiels since 2021; real people Alexander McCall Smith and Andrew Crummy, facts well known to me). Three OG options as in 2.40 and 2.33.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In evolutionary biology, an exaptation is a trait that evolved to serve one function and was later adapted for a different purpose.
• Biologists Stephen Jay Gould and Elisabeth Vrba introduced the term in 1982.
• In mammals’ ancestors, small bones at the back of the jaw formed part of the jaw joint.
• Over millions of years, two of these bones migrated into the middle ear.
• In modern mammals, they transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of an exaptation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Exaptations, a term that Stephen Jay Gould and Elisabeth Vrba introduced in 1982, are traits that evolved to serve one function and were later adapted for a different purpose.
Two small bones that once formed part of the jaw joint in the ancestors of mammals now transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear in modern mammals.
The jaw joint and the middle ear are two examples of exaptations, since both of them transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear in mammals.
An exaptation is a trait that evolved for one function and was later adapted for another, such as two jaw bones of mammals’ ancestors that now help mammals hear.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: what an exaptation is and an instance of one. Choice D gives the definition, a trait that “evolved to serve one function and was later adapted for a different purpose,” and then the jaw bones that “migrated into the middle ear” and now “transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.”

A.why_wrong: It explains the term and who introduced it but gives no example.

B.why_wrong: It describes the jaw bones that moved to the ear but never says what an exaptation is or that these bones are one.

C.why_wrong: It calls the jaw joint and the middle ear two exaptations that both carry sound, but the notes say the jaw bones once “formed part of the jaw joint” and only later “migrated into the middle ear.”

items.notes: Subject: science (exaptation, Gould and Vrba 1982; mammalian middle-ear bones derived from reptile-like ancestors' jaw-joint bones; textbook-accurate, little known to students). Feathers avoided as the canonical example and close to official feather items. PART definition, PART example, FALSE misreading as in 2.16.

fixes: notes trimmed (dropped “several” and “gradually”); explanation quote matched

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Previous research suggested that a dish’s color can influence how its contents taste.
• A team of food scientists investigated whether bowl color affects how salty a soup seems.
• They served an identical soup to 120 volunteers, half in white bowls and half in blue bowls.
• Each participant rated the soup’s saltiness on a scale from 1 to 10.

items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s aim and methodology. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Food scientists found that participants eating soup from blue bowls rated it as noticeably saltier than participants eating from white bowls did.
To learn whether bowl color affects how salty a soup seems, food scientists had volunteers rate one soup served in white or blue bowls.
Building on previous research about the color of dishes, a team of food scientists investigated whether bowl color affects how salty a soup seems.
Food scientists served an identical soup to 120 volunteers, half in white bowls and half in blue bowls, and had each of them rate its saltiness.
items.explanation: The goal asks for both the aim and the method. Choice B gives the aim, to learn whether “bowl color affects how salty a soup seems,” and the method: volunteers rated “an identical soup” served “in white bowls” or “in blue bowls.”

A.recipe: OG (results instead of aim and method)
A.why_wrong: It reports what the study found, not what it set out to learn or how it was done.

C.why_wrong: It gives the scientists’ aim but not how they tested it.

D.why_wrong: It describes how the study was run but not what it was meant to find out.

items.notes: Subject: social science (food perception). Unnamed, generic study; the design and the one figure (120 volunteers) are invented, the general idea (dish color shapes taste) is a real research theme. Aim-and-method goal as in 2.21; PART aim, PART method, OG results.

fixes: first bullet shortened (a dish’s color)

items.subtype: Describe to an audience familiar with the term
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Larder hoarding is a behavior in which an animal accumulates food in a single central stockpile.
• Other animals bury food in numerous small, scattered caches.
• The American red squirrel, a larder hoarder, inhabits the coniferous forests of northern North America.
• Each autumn, it gathers thousands of spruce cones into an enormous heap called a midden.
• The midden’s cool, damp interior prevents the cones from opening and releasing their seeds.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the American red squirrel’s food storage to an audience already familiar with larder hoarding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Each autumn, the American red squirrel, a larder hoarder, gathers thousands of spruce cones into a midden, where cool, damp conditions keep the cones from opening.
A larder hoarder, the American red squirrel accumulates its food in a single central stockpile rather than burying it in numerous small, scattered caches.
The American red squirrel practices larder hoarding, a behavior in which an animal accumulates food in a single central stockpile, such as a midden.
The American red squirrel, a larder hoarder that stores food for later use, inhabits the coniferous forests of northern North America.
items.explanation: An audience that already knows what larder hoarding is can be given the term without a definition, along with the new details. Choice A calls the squirrel “a larder hoarder” without explaining the term and describes how it gathers “thousands of spruce cones” into a midden whose “cool, damp interior prevents the cones from opening.”

B.why_wrong: It spends the sentence explaining what larder hoarding is, which this audience already knows, and gives nothing new about the squirrel’s storage.

C.why_wrong: It defines larder hoarding again for an audience that already understands it.

D.why_wrong: It tells where the squirrel lives but not how it stores its food.

items.notes: Subject: science (American red squirrel middens of spruce cones; well known to me). A live RS EXAMPLE item (sky islands) mentions the Mount Graham red squirrel's habitat, a different subject; nothing there about caching. Two AUD options as in 2.18. Reviewer: kept beside the live Mount Graham red squirrel item (same species, a different subject); the key now names the familiar term unglossed, as 2.18’s key does.

fixes: key A now uses “a larder hoarder” unglossed, as the 2.18 key uses “leporello”; explanation rewritten
kept beside the live Mount Graham red squirrel item (rhetorical_synthesis.EXAMPLE.medium.w2b1_16): same species, different subject (sky-island endemism, not caching)

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The majority of sharks hunt fish, seals, or other sizable prey.
• The whale shark inhabits warm tropical waters and can exceed 50 feet in length.
• It feeds by gulping seawater and filtering out plankton, minuscule organisms that drift with ocean currents.
• The basking shark inhabits cooler temperate waters and can exceed 30 feet in length.
• It swims with its enormous mouth open, straining plankton out of the passing water.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the diets of the whale shark and the basking shark. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: While the whale shark inhabits warm tropical waters, the basking shark inhabits cooler temperate waters.
The whale shark feeds by gulping seawater and filtering out plankton, minuscule organisms that drift with ocean currents.
Unlike most sharks, which hunt sizable prey, the whale shark and the basking shark both feed on plankton, minuscule drifting organisms.
The whale shark can exceed 50 feet in length, while the basking shark, the smaller of the two, can exceed 30 feet.
items.explanation: The two sharks feed in different ways, but the notes say both take in “plankton, minuscule organisms that drift with ocean currents”: the whale shark by “filtering out plankton” and the basking shark by “straining plankton out of the passing water.” Choice C states this shared diet with “both.”

A.why_wrong: It contrasts where the two sharks live; it is about habitat, not diet, and it stresses a difference.

B.why_wrong: It describes the whale shark’s feeding alone, so it shows no similarity.

D.why_wrong: It compares the sharks’ sizes, not their diets.

items.notes: Subject: science (whale and basking sharks, both plankton filter feeders; sizes rounded down). A live TSP item is about whale sharks digesting Sargassum, a different subject. The feeding methods differ, so the shared trait is the diet only.

fixes: basking-shark feeding bullet shortened toward the models’ median; explanation quote matched

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Seeds of most flowering plants ripen above ground.
• Subterranean clover (Trifolium subterraneum) is a small herb native to the Mediterranean.
• After the plant flowers, its stalks bend down and push the young seed heads into the soil, where the seeds ripen.
• The hog peanut (Amphicarpaea bracteata) is a vine of North American woodlands.
• It also grows small flowers near its base that produce seeds underground.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about where some plants’ seeds ripen. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Examples of plants whose seeds ripen underground include subterranean clover of the Mediterranean and the hog peanut of North America.
While subterranean clover pushes its seed heads into the soil, the hog peanut grows small flowers near its base that produce seeds underground.
Subterranean clover, a small Mediterranean herb, pushes its young seed heads into the soil, where the seeds ripen.
Unlike those of most flowering plants, the seeds of some plants ripen underground.
items.explanation: A generalization makes a broad claim drawn from the specific cases. Subterranean clover pushes its seed heads “into the soil, where the seeds ripen,” and the hog peanut grows flowers that “produce seeds underground.” Choice D draws the general pattern from both cases: the seeds of some plants ripen underground.

A.why_wrong: It names two plants whose seeds ripen underground, but it only lists examples; it never draws a broad claim from them.

B.why_wrong: It contrasts how the two plants get their seeds into the ground instead of stating what they show about plants in general.

C.why_wrong: It describes subterranean clover alone, a single specific case rather than a generalization.

items.notes: Subject: science (plants that ripen seeds underground: subterranean clover, Trifolium subterraneum, buries its seed heads; the hog peanut, Amphicarpaea bracteata, sets underground seeds from flowers near its base; standard botany, no named people). Replaced at review: the fire lily and grass tree draft (fire-triggered flowering) sat beside the live RS item on plants recovering after fire (w4b5_03) and the CB fynbos fire-germination item. Key is the short abstract claim, as in 2.12.

fixes: subject replaced (fire-triggered flowering was the same fire-plant concept as live rhetorical_synthesis.DIFF.hard.w4b5_03 and the CB Cross-Text fynbos item); new subject: plants that ripen seeds underground, grepped and claimed; key letter, option shapes and length kept

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Textile artist Marisol Ybarra creates embroidered maps of the San Antonio River and its surrounding neighborhoods.
• She assembles the maps from shirts, dresses, and other clothing contributed by residents of riverside communities.
• “I stitch the river in old blue jeans and the streets in whatever arrives that week,” she explains.
• “Every scrap once belonged to someone who lives on this map,” she says.
• An art critic described her 2019 map of the river as “a deeply personal atlas.”
items.stem: The student wants to provide a quotation from Ybarra that explains why she makes her maps from residents’ clothing. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Ybarra assembles her maps from contributed garments because, as she puts it, “every scrap once belonged to someone who lives on this map.”
An art critic called Ybarra’s 2019 map of the San Antonio River “a deeply personal atlas.”
Ybarra’s embroidered maps of the San Antonio River are assembled from clothing contributed by residents of riverside communities.
Ybarra explains that she stitches “the river in old blue jeans and the streets in whatever arrives that week.”
items.explanation: The goal requires Ybarra’s own words giving her reason for making her maps from residents’ clothing. Her remark that “Every scrap once belonged to someone who lives on this map” explains why the garments matter: the people on the map supply the cloth. Choice A quotes it and ties it to the contributed garments.

B.why_wrong: It quotes a critic’s praise, not Ybarra, and says nothing about why she uses residents’ clothing.

C.why_wrong: It says the maps are made from contributed garments but uses no quotation and gives no reason.

D.why_wrong: It quotes Ybarra, but the words describe how she assigns fabrics to parts of the map, not why she uses residents’ clothing.

items.notes: Subject: arts. Marisol Ybarra is an invented artist with invented quotations (RS: no fact-checking); the name was searched once and no textile artist with it turned up. Shape of 2.29: artist quote that explains why (stem paraphrases the notes' garments as residents' clothing), a second artist quote about technique, an outside quote, a paraphrase.

fixes: notes trimmed (dropped “large”, “garments” to “clothing”); option B shortened and C matched
invented names searched once (Marisol Ybarra): no real person in the field turned up; no change

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items.stem: The student wants to specify what the Hohle Fels flute was made from. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

The Hohle Fels flute, which is at least 35,000 years old, was carved from the wing bone of a griffon vulture.
In 2008, archaeologists recovered twelve fragments of the Hohle Fels flute in a cave in southwestern Germany.
The Hohle Fels flute, among the oldest known musical instruments, has five finger holes and a V-shaped notch.
items.explanation: The goal asks what the flute was made from. The notes say “It was carved from the wing bone of a griffon vulture.” Choice B gives that material.

A.recipe: FALSE (another flute’s material attached to this one)
A.why_wrong: Mammoth ivory was the material of “Several other flutes discovered in nearby caves,” not of the Hohle Fels flute.

C.recipe: OG (when and where it was found)
C.why_wrong: It tells when and where the flute was found, not what it was made from.

D.why_wrong: It describes the flute’s holes and age but not its material.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (the Hohle Fels bone flute, found 2008 in twelve pieces, griffon vulture wing bone, five finger holes, at least 35,000 years old; ivory flutes from nearby caves such as Geissenklösterle; well known to me). One FALSE option misattaching a neighbor's material.

fixes: notes trimmed toward the models’ median (age bullet and notch bullet shortened)

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

Pongal is celebrated each January in Tamil Nadu, while Chuseok is celebrated in Korea each September or October.
During Chuseok, families prepare songpyeon, small rice cakes that are steamed on fragrant pine needles.
Pongal, a harvest festival in southern India, is named for a traditional dish.

items.notes: Subject: social science and culture (Pongal of Tamil Nadu, named for the rice dish; Chuseok and songpyeon rice cakes steamed on pine needles; well known to me). Goal names the dimension (foods) so the shared harvest category is not a second key.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items.stem: The student wants to describe how the Carnac stones are arranged. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Erected by prehistoric communities between about 4500 and 3300 BCE, the Carnac stones stand in Brittany, France.
According to local legend, the more than 3,000 Carnac stones are soldiers who were transformed into stone.
Most of the Carnac stones are arranged in long, straight, parallel rows, with eleven rows in one section stretching about a kilometer.
The Carnac stones, which stand in Brittany, France, include a section called Le Ménec.
items.explanation: The goal is the arrangement of the stones. The notes say “Most of the stones are arranged in long, straight, parallel rows” and that at Le Ménec “eleven rows stretch for approximately a kilometer.” Choice C combines these details.

A.why_wrong: It tells when the stones were erected and where they stand, not how they are arranged.

B.why_wrong: It gives a legend about the stones and their number, not their arrangement.

D.why_wrong: It names one section of the site but does not describe how any of the stones are laid out.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Carnac alignments in Brittany, more than 3,000 standing stones raised before 3000 BCE; Le Ménec with eleven rows about a kilometer long; the soldiers-turned-to-stone legend; well known to me).

items.subtype: Define a term and give an example
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• New words enter English through various processes.
• A back-formation is a word created by removing what appears to be a prefix or suffix from an existing word.
• The verb “edit” is a back-formation from the older noun “editor.”
• Speakers reinterpreted “editor” as if it came from a verb.
• A similar example is “burgle,” which originated from “burglar.”
items.stem: The student wants to define the term “back-formation” and provide an example of one. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
options: New words, such as the verb “edit,” enter English through various processes.
A back-formation is a word created by removing what appears to be a suffix from an existing word, as “edit” was created from the older noun “editor.”
The verb “burgle” originated from the noun “burglar.”
Back-formations are new words that are created by removing parts of words.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: a definition and an example. Choice B defines a back-formation as “a word created by removing what appears to be a prefix or suffix from an existing word” and gives the example of “edit,” formed from “editor.”

A.why_wrong: It mentions “edit” but only says that new words enter English through various processes; it never says what a back-formation is.

C.why_wrong: It gives an example of a back-formation without defining the term or even naming it.

D.why_wrong: It gives a loose definition but no example.

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics: back-formation; edit from editor, burgle from burglar; standard etymology). Two-part goal with the plural “these goals,” as in 1.19.

fixes: notes trimmed toward the easy median (through various processes, as if it came from a verb); option A matched
